title: Logic Pro 11 Update
intro: Logic Pro 11 was the biggest release in years. Session Players, the Chord track, Stem Splitter, ChromaGlow and Flashback Capture between them change how a song gets written, not just how it gets edited. This section is everything worth knowing about the new tools.

tips.t: Session Players are Drummer, extended to bass and keys
tips.d: Create a Session Player track and choose Drummer, Bass Player or Keyboard Player. Each one generates a real, editable performance rather than playing back a loop.

tips.t: Every Session Player region is convertible to MIDI
tips.d: Right‑click the region and choose Convert to MIDI Region. You keep the generated performance and gain full note‑level control.

tips.t: Use the Follow parameter to lock players to each other
tips.d: Set the Bass Player to follow the Drummer's kick, and the Keyboard Player to follow the bass. The three of them lock like a band rather than three separate parts.

tips.t: Session Players respond to region length, so write in sections
tips.d: Give each song section its own region and set complexity and intensity per section. That is how you get a verse that builds into a chorus.

tips.t: Swap the player character without losing your settings
tips.d: The performance settings persist when you change the player, so you can audition every character against the same arrangement in seconds.

tips.t: Set Feel to push or pull against the grid
tips.d: Ahead of the beat for urgency, behind for laid‑back. It is a per‑region setting and it is the single most musical control in the panel.

tips.t: Regenerate a performance without changing anything else
tips.d: Small nudges to complexity or intensity produce a fresh take of the same part. If a phrase is not landing, nudge rather than rebuild.

tips.t: Layer two Session Players on the same part
tips.d: One playing simply, one playing busily, with the busy one low in the mix. Instant realistic double‑tracking.

tips.t: Bass Player follows the Chord track by default
tips.d: Build your progression once on the Chord track and the bassline follows it, including inversions and passing notes.

tips.t: Use the Note Range control to keep the part in a register
tips.d: Constraining the range stops the generated line from jumping octaves and keeps it sitting in the same place in the mix.

tips.t: Adjust the Complexity slider before you adjust anything else
tips.d: It controls how many notes the player uses per bar. Low complexity in a verse and high in a chorus is an arrangement decision made with one slider.

tips.t: Turn on or off specific articulations
tips.d: Slides, hammer‑ons, dead notes and muted notes are individually switchable. Turning slides off alone makes a part sound completely different.

tips.t: Pair Bass Player with Studio Bass for the intended sound
tips.d: The playing engine and the instrument are separate. Studio Bass is the sampled instrument designed to respond to the articulations Bass Player generates.

tips.t: Set the Bass Player to follow a specific track's rhythm
tips.d: Point Follow at your guitar or piano and the bass locks to that rhythm instead of the drums, which is how you get a riff‑driven arrangement.

tips.t: Set the left-hand voicing before anything else
tips.d: Keyboard Player's left hand can play Root Only, Root & Octave or Root & Fifth, and the right hand has its own voicing type plus a movement amount. Same chords, entirely different mood — and it is the fastest way to stop the part fighting your bass.

tips.t: Use the left‑ and right‑hand controls independently
tips.d: You can simplify the left hand and keep the right hand busy, which is how real players comp behind a vocal.

tips.t: Set the rhythmic density separately from the complexity
tips.d: Sparse and complex is a very different thing from busy and simple. Both controls exist for that reason.

tips.t: Convert to MIDI and delete the left hand entirely
tips.d: The fastest route to a usable pad or Rhodes comp is to generate a full part and then remove what you do not need.

tips.t: Use Keyboard Player as a writing tool, not a final part
tips.d: Generate a progression, convert it to MIDI, then play the good bits yourself. The generated part becomes your reference.

tips.t: Try it on a synth patch, not just a piano
tips.d: The performance engine is instrument‑agnostic. Point it at a pad or a pluck and the results are often better than on piano.

tips.t: Show the Chord track in Global Tracks
tips.d: Press G, then enable Chord. Every Session Player and any track you tell to follow it will play the progression you enter.

tips.t: Generate chords from an existing MIDI region
tips.d: Drag a MIDI region onto the Chord track and Logic analyses it and builds the progression for you. Works on audio via the Chord analysis too.

tips.t: Change one chord and hear the whole arrangement follow
tips.d: This is the point of the feature. Swapping a minor for a major in bar 12 updates bass, keys and any following track instantly.

tips.t: Use the Chord track to transpose the whole song correctly
tips.d: Unlike a blanket transpose, chord‑aware transposition keeps voicings musical rather than just shifting everything by semitones.

tips.t: Set chord duration precisely by dragging chord boundaries
tips.d: Chords snap to the grid, so a half‑bar change is a two‑second edit.

tips.t: Turn Follow Chord Track off for parts that should not move
tips.d: Each track has a Follow Chord Track setting in the region inspector. Turn it off for drums, samples and anything already committed.

tips.t: Split any mixed audio into four parts
tips.d: Select an audio region and choose Stem Splitter from the region's contextual menu. Logic separates vocals, drums, bass and other into four new tracks.

tips.t: Use it on your own rough mixes, not just other people's records
tips.d: The most legitimate and useful application is recovering a part from a bounce when the original session is gone.

tips.t: Split first, then process — artefacts are frequency dependent
tips.d: The separated stems have artefacts in predictable places. A gentle high shelf or a de‑esser on the vocal stem cleans up most of it.

tips.t: Use single stems as layers, not as full replacements
tips.d: A split drum stem buried under real drums adds character without exposing the artefacts.

tips.t: Split a loop to remove the element you do not want
tips.d: Delete the vocal stem and you have an instrumental. Delete everything but drums and you have a break.

tips.t: Splitting is non‑destructive to the original
tips.d: Your source region stays untouched on its own track, so you can always start again.

tips.t: ChromaGlow is five saturation models in one plugin
tips.d: Each model has a distinct character. Audition all five before you touch a single control — the model choice matters far more than the settings.

tips.t: Use the Drive and Output together to stay level‑matched
tips.d: Saturation makes things louder, and louder always sounds better. Match levels before you decide whether it is actually helping.

tips.t: Put it on the drum bus before the compressor
tips.d: Saturating transients before compression gives the compressor less to fight and produces a much more controlled result.

tips.t: Use the Detail control for high‑frequency behaviour
tips.d: It adjusts how the saturation treats top end, which is the difference between “warm” and “harsh”.

tips.t: Try it on the master at very low drive
tips.d: A tiny amount across the whole mix does what analogue summing is supposed to do. Anything you can obviously hear is too much.

tips.t: Flashback Capture retrieves what you just played
tips.d: The dedicated button in the control bar — or ⇧R — grabs the MIDI you performed even though you were not recording. A region appears at the playhead containing the performance.

tips.t: ⇧R is already on the keyboard, so build the reflex
tips.d: The whole value of the feature is that it costs nothing to reach for. Hit it the moment you play something you like, before you have decided whether it was any good.

tips.t: It works while the transport is stopped
tips.d: Noodling with the song not playing is exactly when the good ideas arrive. Flashback Capture catches those too, and it captures controller moves as well as notes.

tips.t: Use Mastering Assistant as an analysis tool, not a finisher
tips.d: Run it, look at what it decided to do to your mix, then go and fix those things in the mix itself. Its EQ curve is a free critique of your master bus.

tips.t: Check plugin compatibility after updating
tips.d: Major releases drop support for older plugin formats. Open your three most important old projects and check every insert before you rely on the new version.
